title: Charlie Parker in the band
summary: Cootie calls Parker the most influential jazz musician; Parker left because Cootie only let him solo, not play parts.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Because I mean, in those days, they hadn't really got accepted in those days. I mean, Charlie Parker wasn't really accepted, and certainly Bud Powell wasn't either. The working for you was one of their first big time jobs. Am I not right?
Well, I think so, yeah.
Yeah. I think so.
I think that Charlie Parker was the greatest individual musician that ever lived. You know, influenced musicians.
Was he?
I think he influenced more musicians than any other musician in the history of jazz.
As opposed to what Dizzy -- like when he and Dizzy got together -- as opposed to what Dizzy was contributing, did you feel that Charlie had more of the original -- of the unique concept?
Yeah.
You did?
Uh-huh.
Of course, the horn was easier, to spell it out. It was easier to spell it out on saxophone than it would be to spell it out on trumpet.
But no musicians in that -- musicians in that area, I think they followed Charlie Parker moreso than any musician.
Yeah.
See, you had the drums trying to play like Charlie Parker.
Yeah.
Trombone, every instrument in the band tried to copy Charlie Parker. And in the history of jazz there has never been one man influence all the instruments.
Yeah.
So that's the reason why I said that.
Yeah. Well, that's very interesting. What was Charlie Parker doing when you hired him?
What was Charlie doing then? I don't know. I think Eddie mentioned he went to the Army. He had to go into the Army.
Yeah.
He had to go into the Army.
Yeah.
And that's when I got Charlie Parker.
He was around New York.
Yeah.
Yeah. And that's before he and Dizzy tied up together down on 52nd Street. It was before, I think. Am I not right?
I think so, yeah.
I think so, too. Well, what was he with you, like about a year? Or more?
Yeah. No, about a year.
About a year. Was he happy enough in the band?
Oh, yeah. He was happy. He was happy in the band.
Was he.
The only thing that he didn't like, I wouldn't let him play parts. I had him just as a soloist.
Oh. You wouldn't let him play the parts?
No.
How come?
Well, it seemed like he'd blend in with the rest of the saxophones.
Yeah. He couldn't blend in with them, huh?
No.
No.
And I didn't like that, so I had him --
There for a soloist.
For a soloist. And he didn't like that, so he quit.
(Laughter)
Well, I'll be darned. Isn't that funny? Well, after all, I mean, the way it worked out as far as he was concerned, people had to learn to blend in with him, didn't they?
Yeah.
Well, he was never really a section man
